difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a physician is justified in withholding a treatment option only if (a) the option poses substantial risk to the patient and (b) a safer alternative exists. Correct answer satisfies both parts; traps satisfy only one or reverse the conditional.
stimulus: A physician is justified in withholding a treatment option from a patient only if the option poses a substantial risk to that patient's health and a safer alternative capable of achieving the same therapeutic goal is available. If only one of these conditions is met, withholding the option is not justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A surgeon declines to inform a patient about an experimental procedure that carries a 40 percent chance of serious complications; a conventional surgery with equivalent outcomes and a 5 percent complication rate is available. The surgeon's decision is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cardiologist withholds information about a high-risk intervention because the patient has expressed a general preference not to hear about risky options. No alternative treatment exists. The cardiologist's decision is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A general practitioner does not mention an herbal supplement to a patient because no clinical evidence supports its use, even though a medically recognized treatment is available. The practitioner's decision is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An oncologist omits a chemotherapy regimen from discussion because it offers marginally better outcomes than the standard regimen and both carry similar risk profiles. A safer option with equal efficacy exists. The oncologist's decision is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A neurologist withholds discussion of a surgical option that carries substantial neurological risk; however, no non-surgical treatment can achieve the same outcome. The neurologist's decision is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both antecedents: the withheld option poses a substantial risk (40% serious complications), and a safer alternative achieving the same therapeutic goal is available (conventional surgery, 5% complication rate). The principle's consequent — that withholding is justified — therefore applies.
explanations.A: Correct. Both conditions are met: substantial risk and a safer equivalent alternative.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. There is no safer alternative, so only one condition (substantial risk) might be argued, but the second condition (safer alternative available) is explicitly not met. Withholding is therefore not justified under the principle.
explanations.C: Outside-scope trap. The principle concerns options that pose substantial risk; the herbal supplement is withheld because it lacks evidence, not because it poses substantial risk. The antecedent is not satisfied.
explanations.D: Partial fit / extra-fact misdirection. The rationale for omission is marginal benefit difference, not substantial risk. The similar risk profiles mean the first antecedent (substantial risk) is not satisfied.
explanations.E: Reversed application trap. Only the first condition (substantial risk) is met; the second condition (safer alternative available) is explicitly absent. The principle states both must be present; withholding is not justified.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in a legal/policy domain: an employer is obligated to accommodate a worker's religious practice only if (a) the accommodation does not impose undue hardship on the business and (b) the worker has formally notified the employer of the need. Distractors each fail one condition.
stimulus: An employer is obligated to accommodate an employee's religious practice only when the employee has formally notified the employer of the need for accommodation and the accommodation would not impose undue hardship on the business's operations. Absent either condition, no obligation arises.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A retail manager refuses to adjust a Muslim employee's break schedule to allow Friday prayers, even though the employee submitted a written accommodation request and rescheduling would cost the store nothing. The manager's refusal violates the employer's obligation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A factory supervisor denies a Seventh-day Adventist worker's request to avoid Saturday shifts, citing the difficulty of finding replacements. The worker submitted the request in writing two weeks ago. Because the hardship is undue, no obligation exists, and the supervisor's denial is appropriate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An office manager learns informally that a Jewish employee observes the Sabbath and unilaterally adjusts the schedule, concluding that the adjustment costs nothing. The employee never made a formal request. The manager's action fulfills the employer's obligation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A company declines to permit an employee to wear a religious head covering, noting that no formal policy on religious dress exists. The employee has repeatedly asked verbally. Because no written policy exists, no obligation arises.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A department head accommodates a Hindu employee's request to observe a religious holiday, even though covering the absence requires costly overtime. The head concludes that the moral importance of religious practice always overrides business cost concerns.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies both conditions: the employee formally notified the employer in writing, and the accommodation would impose undue hardship (difficulty finding replacements). When undue hardship exists, the principle confirms no obligation arises, making the denial appropriate and conforming to the principle.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. Both conditions for obligation are met (formal notice, no undue hardship), yet the employer refuses. This scenario illustrates a violation of the principle, not conformance.
explanations.B: Correct. Formal notification was given, but undue hardship exists; therefore no obligation arises. The denial conforms to the principle.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The cost condition is satisfied (no undue hardship), but the employee never formally notified the employer. Only one condition is met, so no obligation exists — the manager's voluntary action cannot 'fulfill an obligation' that hasn't arisen.
explanations.D: Outside-scope / extra-fact misdirection. The principle's trigger is formal notification by the employee, not the existence of a written company policy. The employee's verbal requests may or may not constitute formal notification, but the reasoning given (no written policy) is irrelevant to the principle.
explanations.E: Violates/misapplies-scope trap. The department head acts on a moral override not present in the principle. The principle does not say religious importance overrides cost; it limits obligation to cases of no undue hardship.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in environmental policy: a government agency is justified in imposing an emission fine only if (a) the facility exceeded its permitted emission level and (b) the facility had been given prior written notice of the violation. Traps satisfy only one condition or invert the rule.
stimulus: A government environmental agency is justified in imposing a fine on an industrial facility for emissions violations only if the facility's recorded emissions exceeded its permitted level during the relevant period and the agency had previously issued the facility a written notice of violation. Unless both conditions are satisfied, imposition of the fine is not justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An agency fines a chemical plant after finding its sulfur dioxide output 30 percent above the permitted ceiling. The agency had sent the plant a written violation notice the previous quarter. The fine is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An agency fines a power station whose nitrogen oxide emissions were within permitted limits, on the grounds that the station had received a prior written notice related to a different pollutant. The fine is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An agency fines a refinery that exceeded its permitted emission level last year, even though the refinery received only a verbal warning at the time and no written notice was ever issued. The fine is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agency declines to fine a smelting facility that exceeded permitted emission levels, because the agency had already issued a written notice and considers one enforcement action sufficient. The agency's restraint is justified under the principle.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An agency issues a written notice to a factory whose emissions are currently within permitted limits, in anticipation of future violations. Because the notice was properly issued, any subsequent fine would be justified regardless of future emission levels.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both antecedents: the facility's recorded emissions exceeded the permitted level (30% above ceiling), and the agency had previously issued a written notice of violation. Both conditions being met, the principle confirms the fine is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Emissions exceeded permitted level AND prior written notice was given — both conditions satisfied.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The written notice was for a different pollutant; the current emissions are within permitted limits. The first condition (exceeding permitted level for the relevant period) is not satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The facility exceeded permitted levels, but only a verbal warning was given — not a written notice of violation. The second condition is not met, so the fine is not justified under the principle.
explanations.D: Outside-scope / violates-principle trap. Both conditions are met (exceeded levels + written notice), yet the agency declines to fine. The principle says the fine is justified when both are met; it does not say fining is mandatory, but the reasoning given (prior notice makes further action unnecessary) is not supported by the principle and misapplies it.
explanations.E: Reversed/extra-fact trap. The principle requires that emissions actually exceeded permitted levels during the relevant period before a fine is justified. A prospective notice cannot pre-authorize a future fine regardless of future emission levels; that inverts the principle's structure.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in ethics/education: a teacher is warranted in reporting a student's misconduct to administration only if (a) the misconduct poses a risk of harm to other students and (b) the teacher has first attempted to resolve the matter directly with the student. Traps address only one condition.
stimulus: A teacher is warranted in reporting a student's misconduct to the school administration only if the misconduct poses a genuine risk of harm to other students and the teacher has first made a good-faith attempt to resolve the matter directly with the student. If only one of these conditions obtains, reporting to administration is not warranted.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A history teacher reports a student to the principal for repeatedly talking during lectures after speaking with the student privately twice. Because disruption harms classroom learning, the teacher's report is warranted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A science teacher discovers that a student has been tampering with lab equipment in ways that could injure classmates. After a private conversation with the student yields no change in behavior, the teacher reports the matter to the administration. The report is warranted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A gym teacher, alarmed that a student threatened a classmate, immediately reports the threat to the principal without speaking to the student first, reasoning that the risk of harm is too serious to delay. The report is warranted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An art teacher reports a student for plagiarizing a class project, having spoken with the student about the issue, because plagiarism ultimately harms the academic community. The report is warranted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A math teacher attempts to resolve a cheating incident directly with a student but, finding the conversation unproductive, reports the student to administration. Because the teacher made a good-faith attempt first, the report is warranted.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies both conditions: tampering with lab equipment poses a genuine risk of harm to other students (physical injury), and the teacher made a good-faith direct attempt to resolve the matter before reporting. Both antecedents are met, so reporting is warranted.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. The teacher did attempt direct resolution (two private conversations), but talking during lectures does not constitute a genuine risk of harm to other students as the principle requires. Only the second condition is met.
explanations.B: Correct. Risk of physical harm to classmates (first condition) and prior direct conversation (second condition) are both satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The risk of harm condition is met (a threat to a classmate), but the teacher skipped the direct-resolution attempt entirely. Only the first condition is satisfied; the report is not warranted under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / outside-scope trap. The teacher did speak with the student first, but plagiarism harming the 'academic community' is not equivalent to posing a genuine risk of harm to other students as specified in the principle. The first condition is not clearly satisfied.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. A good-faith direct attempt was made, satisfying the second condition. However, cheating (as described) does not pose a genuine risk of harm to other students; the first condition is not met. The teacher's reasoning conflates procedural compliance with full satisfaction of the principle.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in economics/consumer protection: a consumer is entitled to a full refund only if (a) the product failed to perform its advertised function and (b) the consumer returns the product within the warranty period. Distractors fail one condition or misapply the consequent.
stimulus: A consumer is entitled to a full refund on a purchased product only if the product failed to perform the function advertised by the manufacturer and the consumer returns the product within the manufacturer's stated warranty period. If either condition is not met, the consumer is not entitled to a full refund.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yolanda purchases a blender advertised as capable of crushing ice. Within the warranty period, she finds it can crush ice but dislikes the noise level. She returns it and demands a full refund. She is entitled to the refund.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marcus buys a waterproof watch advertised as water-resistant to 50 meters. The watch stops functioning after brief submersion at 10 meters. He returns it three months after the one-year warranty expired. He is entitled to a full refund.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Priya purchases a space heater advertised to heat rooms up to 400 square feet. The heater fails to warm her 300-square-foot room. She returns it within the warranty period. She is entitled to a full refund.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tomás buys a printer advertised as compatible with his operating system. After the warranty expires, he discovers it was never compatible. He returns it promptly. He is entitled to a full refund.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renata returns a coffee maker within the warranty period because she prefers a different brand. The machine brews coffee exactly as advertised. She is entitled to a full refund because she acted within the warranty period.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies both conditions: the heater failed to perform its advertised function (heating rooms up to 400 sq ft, but failing to heat a smaller 300 sq ft room), and Priya returned it within the warranty period. Both antecedents are met, so she is entitled to a full refund.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. Yolanda returned the blender within the warranty period (second condition met), but the blender did perform its advertised function — crushing ice. She is dissatisfied for a reason unrelated to the advertised function, so the first condition is not met.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The watch failed to perform its advertised function (first condition met), but Marcus returned it after the warranty expired. The second condition is not satisfied; he is not entitled to a refund.
explanations.C: Correct. Both conditions satisfied: advertised function failed and return within warranty period.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The printer failed to perform its advertised function (first condition met), but Tomás returns it after the warranty has expired. The second condition is not met; no entitlement arises.
explanations.E: Partial fit / violates-principle trap. Renata returned within the warranty period (second condition met), but the product performed exactly as advertised. The first condition is not met; she is not entitled to a full refund under the principle.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in technology/privacy policy: a data company is obligated to delete a user's personal data upon request only if (a) the data was collected without the user's explicit consent and (b) the user can demonstrate that retaining the data causes ongoing harm to the user. Traps satisfy only one condition.
stimulus: A technology company is obligated to delete a user's personal data upon request only if the data was originally collected without the user's explicit consent and the user can demonstrate that continued retention of the data causes the user ongoing harm. If only one of these conditions is satisfied, no deletion obligation exists.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A user requests deletion of browsing data that was collected after the user clicked 'I agree' to the site's data policy. The user argues that retaining the data is embarrassing. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A user discovers that a social-media platform collected location data without any consent notification. The user shows that advertisers are using the data to target the user with content that aggravates the user's anxiety disorder. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A user requests deletion of purchase-history data collected without consent. The user cannot identify any specific harm from its retention but objects on principle. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A user requests deletion of health data that was collected with full explicit consent. The user demonstrates that a data breach has caused the user's insurance premiums to rise. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A user requests deletion of email data that was collected without consent. The company argues that deletion would be technically burdensome. Because deletion is burdensome, the company has no obligation to delete.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies both conditions: the location data was collected without any consent notification (no explicit consent), and the user demonstrates ongoing harm — advertisers using the data aggravate the user's anxiety disorder. Both antecedents are met; the company is obligated to delete.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. The user clicked 'I agree,' giving explicit consent; the first condition is not satisfied. The company has no deletion obligation regardless of the embarrassment claim.
explanations.B: Correct. No consent was given, and ongoing harm is demonstrated. Both conditions are met.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. Data was collected without consent (first condition met), but the user cannot identify any specific ongoing harm. The second condition is not satisfied; no obligation exists.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The data breach demonstrates ongoing harm (second condition met), but the data was collected with full explicit consent. The first condition is not met; no obligation exists under the principle.
explanations.E: Outside-scope / extra-fact trap. Technical burden is not a condition addressed by the principle. The principle's conditions concern consent and harm; the company's technical difficulty is irrelevant to whether the obligation exists.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in arts/intellectual property: a court should award damages to an artist for unauthorized reproduction of a work only if (a) the reproduction was made for commercial gain and (b) the artist had registered the work with the appropriate copyright authority before the reproduction occurred. Distractors fail one condition.
stimulus: A court should award damages to an artist for unauthorized reproduction of the artist's work only if the reproduction was made for commercial gain by the reproducing party and the artist had registered the work with the appropriate copyright authority prior to the unauthorized reproduction. If either condition is absent, an award of damages is not appropriate.
questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A graphic novelist's work was reproduced without authorization in a for-profit merchandise line. The artist had registered the copyright two years before the reproduction. A court awards damages to the artist.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sculptor's work was photographed without permission and displayed on a nonprofit museum's website with no admission charge. The sculptor had registered the work before the photograph was taken. A court awards damages to the sculptor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A photographer's images were used without authorization in a commercial advertising campaign. The photographer registered the copyright three months after the campaign launched. A court awards damages to the photographer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A composer's melody was reproduced commercially without consent. The composer had not registered the work at the time of reproduction but registered it the following year. A court awards damages to the composer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A painter's work was reproduced without consent in a for-profit art book. The painter had not yet registered the copyright at the time of reproduction. Because the reproduction generated substantial revenue, a court awards damages to the painter.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: the reproduction was made for commercial gain (for-profit merchandise line), and the artist had registered the copyright prior to the reproduction (two years before). Both antecedents are met; the damages award is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Commercial gain and prior registration are both present.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The sculptor had prior registration (second condition met), but the museum's display was nonprofit with no admission charge — the first condition (commercial gain) is not satisfied. Damages are not appropriate under the principle.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The reproduction was for commercial gain (first condition met), but registration occurred three months after the campaign launched — not prior to the reproduction. The second condition is not met; damages are not appropriate.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The reproduction was commercial (first condition met), but the composer had not registered the work before the reproduction. Post-hoc registration does not satisfy the principle's prior-registration requirement.
explanations.E: Partial fit / extra-fact trap. The reproduction was for commercial gain (first condition met), but the painter had not registered the copyright before the reproduction occurred. Revenue generated is irrelevant to the principle; the second condition is not satisfied.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in linguistics/academic policy: a journal editor is justified in rejecting a submitted manuscript without external peer review only if (a) the manuscript falls entirely outside the journal's stated scope and (b) the manuscript contains no original empirical data. Traps satisfy only one condition or misread the consequent.
stimulus: A journal editor is justified in rejecting a submitted manuscript without sending it to external peer reviewers only if the manuscript falls entirely outside the journal's stated subject-matter scope and the manuscript contains no original empirical data. If either condition is not met, the manuscript must be sent to external peer review before a rejection decision.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An editor at a linguistics journal receives a manuscript on quantum physics that includes a novel dataset of particle-collision measurements. The editor rejects it without peer review, reasoning that quantum physics is outside the journal's scope.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An editor at a history journal receives a purely theoretical essay arguing for a new periodization of the Renaissance; it contains no original empirical data. The essay addresses Renaissance history, which is within the journal's scope. The editor rejects it without peer review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An editor at an economics journal receives a manuscript on marine biology that reviews existing literature but includes no new datasets or original observations. The editor rejects it without peer review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An editor at a medical journal receives a manuscript on pharmacology — squarely within scope — with original clinical trial data. The editor finds the methodology weak and rejects it without peer review.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An editor at a sociology journal receives a manuscript on cultural anthropology — adjacent to but not within the journal's scope — that includes original survey data. The editor sends it to peer review before deciding. The editor's decision is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies both conditions: marine biology is entirely outside an economics journal's stated scope, and the manuscript contains no original empirical data (reviews only existing literature). Both antecedents are met; rejection without peer review is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. Quantum physics is outside a linguistics journal's scope (first condition met), but the manuscript contains a novel dataset of original empirical data. The second condition is not satisfied; the manuscript must go to peer review.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The manuscript contains no original empirical data (second condition met), but Renaissance history is within the history journal's scope. The first condition is not met; the editor must send it to peer review.
explanations.C: Correct. Marine biology is outside an economics journal's scope AND no original empirical data is present. Both conditions satisfied.
explanations.D: Violates-principle trap. Pharmacology is within the medical journal's scope, so the first condition fails immediately. Sending the manuscript out — or in this case wrongly rejecting it without review — is not justified by the principle regardless of methodological concerns.
explanations.E: Outside-scope / conforms-to-different-outcome trap. The editor sends the manuscript to peer review, which is actually the correct action under the principle when a condition is not met (original data is present). This scenario is consistent with the principle but asks whether peer review is justified, not whether rejection without review is — a subtle mismatch with the principle's framing, and it doesn't describe a rejection decision.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in history/governance: a head of state is morally justified in declaring a state of emergency only if (a) a threat to national security that cannot be addressed through ordinary legislative means is imminent and (b) the declaration is submitted for legislative ratification within 72 hours. Traps miss one condition.
stimulus: A head of state is morally justified in declaring a state of emergency only if an imminent threat to national security exists that cannot be adequately addressed through ordinary legislative processes and the declaration is submitted to the legislature for ratification within seventy-two hours of issuance. Both conditions must be satisfied for the declaration to be morally justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Facing an imminent cyberattack on critical infrastructure that legislators cannot convene quickly enough to address, a president declares a state of emergency and submits it to the legislature for ratification 48 hours later. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prime minister declares a state of emergency in response to widespread labor strikes, arguing that normal legislative debate would take too long. The declaration is submitted for ratification after 96 hours. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alarmed by a sudden economic downturn, a president declares a state of emergency and submits it for legislative ratification within 24 hours. The legislature could have convened an emergency session to address the downturn ordinarily. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chancellor declares a state of emergency in response to a terrorist organization's credible threat of imminent attacks on multiple cities. The threat cannot be addressed through ordinary legislation in time. The chancellor submits the declaration for ratification after one week. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Responding to a severe flood that kills dozens, a governor declares a state of emergency. An emergency legislative session could have been convened to authorize relief funds within hours. The declaration is submitted for ratification within 12 hours. The governor's declaration is morally justified.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: an imminent national security threat (cyberattack on critical infrastructure) exists that cannot be addressed through ordinary legislative means (legislators cannot convene quickly enough), and the declaration was submitted for ratification within 72 hours (48 hours). Both antecedents are met.
explanations.A: Correct. Imminent security threat unaddressable by ordinary legislation, and ratification submitted within 72 hours.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. Labor strikes may not constitute an imminent national security threat in the principle's sense, and critically, the declaration was submitted after 96 hours — exceeding the 72-hour window. The second condition is not met.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The declaration was submitted within 24 hours (second condition met), but the legislature could have addressed the economic downturn through ordinary legislative processes. The first condition (ordinary means insufficient) is not satisfied.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The imminent terrorist threat unaddressable by ordinary legislation satisfies the first condition, but the declaration was submitted after one week — far exceeding the 72-hour requirement. The second condition is not met.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The declaration was submitted within 72 hours (second condition met), but an emergency legislative session could have been convened ordinarily within hours. The first condition (threat cannot be adequately addressed through ordinary legislative processes) is not satisfied.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in policy/social ethics: a city government is justified in demolishing a privately owned historic structure only if (a) the structure poses a documented and imminent public safety hazard and (b) the owner has been given reasonable opportunity to remediate the hazard but failed to do so. Distractors each omit one condition.
stimulus: A city government is justified in demolishing a privately owned historic structure only if the structure poses a documented, imminent hazard to public safety and the property owner has been given reasonable opportunity to remediate the hazard but has failed to do so within the time allotted. If either condition is unmet, demolition is not justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city demolishes a century-old warehouse whose crumbling façade poses an imminent risk of collapse onto a busy pedestrian street. The city gave the owner 60 days to make repairs; the owner made no repairs and the deadline passed. The demolition is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A city demolishes a historic theater that engineers have cited as structurally unsound. The city notified the owner of the hazard but demolished the building the next morning before the owner had any opportunity to respond. The demolition is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A city demolishes a Victorian mansion that neighborhood residents consider an eyesore. The city provided the owner 90 days to restore the façade, but the owner declined. Because the owner was given ample time, the demolition is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A city demolishes a historic mill building whose foundation inspectors believe may become hazardous within the next decade. The owner was given 30 days to remediate and failed to act. The demolition is justified because the owner had opportunity to remediate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A city demolishes a landmarked bridge that poses an imminent collapse risk to motorists. Because the bridge is publicly owned, the city proceeds without notifying any private party. The demolition is justified under the same principle.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: the structure poses a documented, imminent public safety hazard (crumbling façade, imminent collapse risk over a pedestrian street), and the owner was given reasonable opportunity (60 days) to remediate but failed to act within the allotted time. Both antecedents are met; demolition is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Imminent documented hazard and reasonable opportunity to remediate with owner's failure to act both present.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The structure poses an imminent hazard (first condition met), but the owner was given no reasonable opportunity to remediate — the building was demolished the following morning. The second condition is not satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The owner was given reasonable opportunity and failed to act (second condition met), but aesthetic concerns — being an 'eyesore' — do not constitute a documented, imminent public safety hazard. The first condition is not met.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The owner was given opportunity to remediate (second condition met), but the foundation hazard is prospective — becoming hazardous within the next decade — not imminent. The first condition (documented, imminent hazard) is not satisfied.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle concerns privately owned historic structures and notification of the private owner. A publicly owned bridge involves no private owner, so the principle's conditions (particularly giving the owner opportunity to remediate) cannot apply. The scenario is outside the principle's scope.
